value.question: How are mean wind speed and wind extremes projected to change in intensity and frequency over South Asia (SAS) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: For South Asia (SAS), there is medium confidence that mean surface wind speed is not projected to decline in the future, as it is an exception to the declining trend observed across most of Asia. Regarding wind extremes, tropical cyclones in Asia are projected to have decreasing frequency and increasing intensity overall, with medium confidence. However, there is limited evidence for projections of changes in other severe wind storms.

This marked dust increase has been associated with drought conditions in the Fertile Crescent (Notaro et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2015), likely amplified by anthropogenic warming (Kelley et al., 2015; Chapter 10). While dust activity has decreased greatly over EAS, current climate models are unable to reproduce the trends (Guan et al., 2015, 2017; Zha et al., 2017; C. Wu et al., 2018). Thus, there is limited evidence for future trends of sand and dust storms in Asia. In conclusion, surface wind speeds have been decreasing in Asia (high confidence), but there is a large uncertainty in future trends. value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Western and Central Europe (WCE) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Western and Central Europe (WCE), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase. This increase is considered "Virtually certain" when compared to both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes (TXx events). Specifically, these models project median increases in 50-year TXx events of more than 0.5°C, 1.5°C, and 5.5°C compared to the 1°C warming level. They also project median increases in annual TXx of more than 2°C, 3°C, and 6°C compared to pre-industrial levels. Generally, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with rising global warming levels. Changes in the intensity of extremes are projected to be at least double at 2°C and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, relative to changes at 1.5°C of global warming. In most regions, future changes in the intensity of temperature extremes will "very likely" be proportional to changes in global warming, and up to two to three times larger, with "high confidence".

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over South Asia (SAS) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In South Asia (SAS), there is high confidence that heavy precipitation is projected to intensify. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in both the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. Specifically, compared to the 1°C warming level, a median increase of more than 25% is projected for the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events. Compared to pre-industrial levels, a median increase of more than 30% is projected for annual Rx1day and Rx5day events, and more than 25% for annual Rx30day events. A detectable increase in extreme precipitation over South Asia can result from a half-degree difference in warming between the 1.5°C and 2.0°C warming levels.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Western and Central Europe (WCE) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Western and Central Europe (WCE), extreme precipitation is projected to increase with high confidence. The intensification of heavy precipitation is projected to be "Very likely" when compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and "Extremely likely" when compared with pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models project an increase in both the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation in WCE.

cited_chunks.text: Western and Central Europe (WCE) regions are affected by pluvial flooding and less than 10% of city areas in the northern and western coastal cities. Projections based on multiple lines of evidence from global to convective permitting model scales show high confidence in extreme precipitation increase in the northern, central and eastern European regions (NEU, WCE, EEU) and in the Alpine area. Increases with medium confidence are projected for the Mediterranean basin (with a negative gradient towards the south) for mid- and end-century under RCP4.5, RCP8.5 and SSP5-8.5 and for 2°C GWL and higher (Section 11.9; MedECC, 2020).
